Summary: The paper proposes adaptive Time Delay Stability (aTDS), a set of data-driven rules for the three sample-counted TDS parameters. (1) The window holds about 30 effectively independent samples of the slowest signal, using a first-zero-truncated Bartlett variance-inflation factor justified by a Cauchy-Schwarz bound. (2) The lag range is (L-1)/2, the aliasing limit of the circular cross-correlation, capped at half a detected rhythm period. (3) The tolerance is the widest one whose chance score on circularly rotated copies (mean + 2 SE) stays within a 5% false-stability budget. A Bayley-Hammersley-type variant (aTDS-BH) gives longer windows. The method is compared with the published setting (60/+-30/+-1), hand-rescaled and estimated-rescaled settings, a labelled oracle, and full-record cross-correlation/GCC-PHAT. Synthetic tests cover AR(1) slow-down benchmarks, fGn, AR(2) rhythms, Rulkov maps, mixed-speed, changing-dynamics, regime-switching, nonlinear and drifting-delay signals, and networks with rotation p-values and BH-FDR. Real-data tests cover the original EEG benchmark pair, a 35-subject polysomnography cohort, and hydrology, energy and fuel-price records. Main findings: aTDS strongly outperforms the fixed published setting on slow systems and avoids a silent wrong-delay failure of a fixed lag range. Default aTDS is statistically equivalent to rescaling the published setting by an estimated correlation time. aTDS-BH detects slow and long-memory coupling better, mainly through longer windows. Full-record estimators are better for constant delays, and no gain is found on the sleep cohort.
Strengths: Addresses a real reproducibility problem: TDS parameters are counted in samples and tuned for 1-Hz sleep data, so their meaning silently changes with sampling rate and system time scale.

Clearly demonstrates a silent failure mode of fixed TDS: when the true delay lies beyond the +-30 lag range, scores stay high (72-96%) while the reported delays are wrong, sometimes with the wrong sign. This is useful to practitioners regardless of aTDS.

Each rule has an explicit statistical rationale (effective sample size, aliasing limit, surrogate calibration against a false-stability budget), and the procedure is fully label-free and algorithmically specified.

Very thorough and fair evaluation with strong baselines (true and estimated rescaling, oracle, full-record XCorr/GCC-PHAT), bootstrap CIs, TOST equivalence tests, Wilson intervals, a one-at-a-time sensitivity analysis of all design constants, and held-out validation of aTDS-BH.

Exceptionally candid reporting of negative results: equivalence with simple rescaling, inferiority to full-record estimators for constant delays, no gain on sleep networks, a seasonal-catchment failure, and budget exceedance near regime boundaries.

Concrete practical guidance (caps below rhythmic periods, supplying dmax, reporting chance levels, per-link FDR-controlled p-values) and good reproducibility (fixed seeds, released code and raw outputs).
Weaknesses: Limited novelty and limited demonstrated advantage. Default aTDS is statistically equivalent to rescaling the published setting by an estimated correlation time, a one-line heuristic, and no synthetic test shows it doing better. Its only edge rests on a single hourly rainfall-runoff record.

aTDS-BH was selected on the benchmark, and its gain is reproduced by first-zero aTDS with 60 instead of 30 effective samples. The window contribution therefore reduces largely to 'longer windows detect always-on coupling better'. The BH factor (variance inflation of a sample mean) is weakly motivated for cross-correlation, and its out-of-distribution validation is limited.

The dominant design constant (30 effective samples) is a convention, and it is the parameter that matters most in the sensitivity analysis. The arbitrariness of the original setting is partly moved rather than removed.

Calibrated tolerances become very wide (up to +-56 samples, sometimes larger than the delay). This dilutes the meaning of a 'stable delay' and makes aTDS scores incomparable with published TDS values, which undercuts the reproducibility motivation. In isolation, tolerance calibration gives no significant AUC gain.

The rotation null destroys shared slow co-modulation, and the SE treats correlated rotations as independent. Both bias toward wider tolerances and anti-conservative p-values. The 5% budget controls only a mean and is exceeded for aTDS-BH, near regime boundaries (8-11%) and on single recordings (95th percentile up to 20%). Block, IAAFT and multivariate nulls are not evaluated.

There is no benefit in the motivating domain. In the 35-subject sleep cohort, no adaptive setting improves stage contrasts, the wake contrast weakens, and the automatic window is too long to resolve stages without a manual cap.

Real-data transfer evidence is anecdotal: single records with very few windows, reference delays partly defined by full-record cross-correlation (circular), one catchment failure, and an uninformative fuel-price record.

The time-resolved setting, the main reason to prefer TDS over full-record estimators, is tested in only one synthetic regime-switching design. There the simple estimated rescaling has much lower false stability (2.0% vs 8.1%). A sliding-window GCC-PHAT or windowed cross-correlation competitor is missing.
All main results use a non-causal stability anchor, which changes the benchmark score substantially (58.1% vs 43.6%). The conclusions are not checked with the original causal anchor.

The theory is loose. The Bartlett/Cauchy-Schwarz bound applies to independent series and full sums, but the estimator truncates at the first zero crossing (ignoring negative and seasonal lobes) and is applied to coupled series. For long-memory signals the factor depends on record length.

There are internal inconsistencies, for example tau_max = 367 for L = 1059 in Table 7, a Limitations sentence that conflicts with Table 5, and the estimated rescaling equalling the published setting for fGn without explanation. The presentation is dense, has many variants and reads like an experiment log. The manuscript was LLM-drafted and, by disclosure, not reviewed by a human expert.
Questions: Given that default aTDS is equivalent to the estimated rescaling, in what concrete setting should a practitioner prefer aTDS? Can you show a synthetic or real case where it is better with statistical support (for example mixed-speed networks or rhythmic signals)?

Since aTDS-BH's gain is matched by first-zero aTDS with 60 effective samples, why propose the BH factor rather than a larger constant with a user-specified time-resolution cap? Is there a setting where BH beats the 60-sample rule?
How do the main conclusions (slow-down AUCs, sleep contrasts, real-record delays) change with the causal stability anchor that reproduces the original 43.6% benchmark value?

How does the tolerance calibration behave under a null that preserves shared slow co-modulation (block or IAAFT bivariate surrogates) and with a recording-clustered SE, particularly on the sleep cohort? Could you calibrate a per-recording upper quantile instead of the mean?
Can the tolerance be tied to the expected variance of the delay estimate (for example Carter's bounds), so that scores stay interpretable and comparable across settings?
How does aTDS compare with sliding-window GCC-PHAT or windowed cross-correlation plus a surrogate test?
How was tau_max = 367 obtained for L = 1059 on catchment L0123002? Why does the estimated rescaling equal the published setting for fGn H = 0.6/0.75?
How robust are the real-record delays to the rotation seeds and to modest window changes, given only 12-46 windows?
Limitations: Default aTDS has no statistically supported advantage over a simple correlation-time rescaling. aTDS-BH's gains come mainly from longer windows, at the cost of time resolution.
Full-record estimators outperform aTDS for constant, always-on delays, and correlation-based TDS misses non-monotone coupling. Pairwise TDS cannot separate direct from indirect coupling.
Long windows leak stability across regime boundaries and cannot resolve short sleep stages without a user-chosen cap. Delays beyond half the window are silently missed unless dmax is supplied.
The false-stability budget controls only a mean. The rotation null and the independent-rotation SE are likely anti-conservative under shared slow co-modulation, so per-link testing is required.
The first-zero Bartlett estimator ignores seasonal and rhythmic lobes and depends on record length for long-memory signals. aTDS scores are not comparable with published TDS scores.

Real-data validation is limited to a few single records and a sleep cohort without ground truth, where no improvement was seen. The societal risk is mild: wide tolerances and high scores could be over-interpreted as strong physiological coupling in clinical studies. The LLM-drafted manuscript calls for extra verification of its numbers.
